q-48580.name: Question 1
q-48580.problem:
Find the value of the constant $b$ that make the function $g(x)$ below continuous at $x=1.$

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}x-2, & x\le 1 \\ {b}^{2}+2xb, & x>1\end{aligned}
$$
q-48580.worked_solution:
At $x=1,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}g(x) & =g(1) \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}({b}^{2}+2xb) \\  & ={b}^{2}+2(1)b \\  & ={b}^{2}+2b.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=1,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}g(x) \\ -1 & ={b}^{2}+2b \\ {b}^{2}+2b+1 & =0 \\ (b+1)^{2} & =0 \\ \sqrt{(b+1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{0} \\ |b+1| & =0 \\ b & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)$ is continuous at $x=1$ for $b=-1.$

q-37914.name: Question 3
q-37914.problem:
Find the value of the constant $k$ that make the function $f(x)$ below continuous at $x=-1.$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}k{x}^{2}+5x-2k, & x\le -1 \\ 4x+3, & x>-1\end{aligned}
$$
q-37914.worked_solution:
At $x=-1,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{-}}f(x) & =f(-1) \\  & =k{(-1)}^{2}+5(-1)-2k \\  & =k-5-2k \\  & =-k-5,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}(4x+3) \\  & =4(-1)+3 \\  & =-4+3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {(-1)}^{+}}f(x) \\ -k-5 & =-1 \\ -k & =4 \\ k & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$ for $k=-4.$

q-4590.name: Question 4
q-4590.problem:
Find the values of the constants $a$ and $b$ that make the function $g(x)$ below continuous at $x=-2$ and $x=0.$

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-x, & x\le -2 \\ a{x}^{2}+b, & -2<x<0 \\ 6, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$
q-4590.worked_solution:
At $x=-2,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}g(x) & =g(-2) \\  & =-(-2) \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}(a{x}^{2}+b) \\  & =a(-2)^{2}+b \\  & =4a+b.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-2,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}g(x) \\ 2 & =4a+b\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, at $x=0,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}(a{x}^{2}+b) \\  & =a(0)^{2}+b \\  & =0+b \\  & =b,\end{aligned}
$$

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}g(x) & =g(0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=0,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}g(x) \\ b & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's solve the following system of equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4a+b=2 \\ b=6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can replace $b$ by $6$ in the first equation. Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4a+b & =2 \\ 4a+6 & =2 \\ 4a & =-4 \\ a & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)$ is continuous at $x=-2$ and $x=0$ for $a=-1$ and $b=6.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x) \\ -5 & =-2a+3b \\ 2a-3b & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the value of the constant $c$ that makes the function $h(x)$ below continuous at $x=2.$

$$
h(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{3}^{cx}\,\,, & x\le 2 \\ {x}^{5}-5, & x>2\end{aligned}
$$
q-76013.worked_solution:
At $x=2,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}h(x) & =h(2) \\  & ={3}^{c(2)} \\  & ={3}^{2c},\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}h(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}({x}^{5}-5) \\  & ={2}^{5}-5 \\  & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $h(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2c} & =27 \\ {3}^{2c} & ={3}^{3} \\ 2c & =3 \\ c & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $h(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$ for $c=\frac{3}{2}.$

$$

$$

 

Therefore, $g(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$ for $a=\frac{1}{4}.$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(cx-4), & \frac{2}{3}<x\le 1 \\ 2x-1, & x>1\end{aligned}
$$

 
is continuous at $x=1,$ find the value of $c.$

At $x=1,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & =f(1) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(c(1)-4) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(c-4),\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(2x-1) \\  & =2(1)-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) \\ {log}_{2}⁡(c-4) & =1 \\ c-4 & ={2}^{1} \\ c & =2+4 \\ c & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the function g(x)={ln⁡(ax),0<x≤32x−6,x>3 is continuous at x=3, find the value of a.

a
1
b
23
c
2
d
3
e
13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At x=3, the left-sided limit is limx→3−g(x)=g(3)=ln⁡(3a),

and the right-sided limit is limx→3+g(x)=limx→3+(2x−6)=2(3)−6=0.

In order for g(x) to be continuous at x=3, we require that limx→3−g(x)=limx→3+g(x)ln⁡(3a)=03a=1a=13.

q-108125.name: Question 19
q-108125.problem:
Given that the function

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2}-b), & 2<x\le 4 \\ 4-x, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

 
is continuous at  $x=4,$ find the value of $b.$
q-108125.worked_solution:
At $x=4,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{-}}g(x) & =g(4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{2}-b) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-b),\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}(4-x) \\  & =4-4 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=4,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}g(x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2-b) & =0 \\ 2-b & =1 \\ b & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-108127.name: Question 20
q-108127.problem:
Given that the function

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡(x+a), & -6\le x\le 2 \\ x-1, & x>2\end{aligned}
$$

 
is continuous at  $x=2,$ find the value of $a.$
q-108127.worked_solution:
At $x=2,$ the left-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}g(x) & =g(2)=\operatorname{log}⁡(2+a),\end{aligned}
$$

 

and the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}(x-1) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we require that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}g(x) \\ \operatorname{log}⁡(2+a) & =1 \\ 2+a & ={10}^{1} \\ 2+a & =10 \\ a & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
